key_insight: Fixing hidden dataset biases (e.g., overlap between training and test molecules/targets) markedly improves how well binding-affinity models generalize to new compounds and targets.
problem_solved: Many binding-affinity models report overly optimistic performance because biased dataset splits let models memorize artifacts instead of learning true biophysical signals; this paper addresses how to detect and remove those biases to obtain realistic generalization estimates.
method: Diagnose common sources of dataset bias (molecule/target overlap, scaffold leakage, label distribution shifts) using targeted partitioning analyses.
Create and evaluate debiased data splits or reweighting procedures that minimize overlap and distributional leakage between train and test sets.
Reassess published models and benchmarks under unbiased evaluation protocols to quantify true generalization gains.
impact: Provides practical guidelines and validation protocols that make binding-affinity predictions more reliable and reproducible, helping practitioners build models that transfer to novel drug discovery scenarios.
visual_elements: Flowchart showing biased vs. debiased data-splitting pipeline (highlighting overlap removal)
Before-and-after bar chart of model performance (biased split vs. debiased split)
Schematic illustrating examples of leakage (same scaffold in train and test) and its effect on learned shortcuts
Checklist infographic of recommended best practices for dataset curation and evaluation
paper_title: Addendum: Resolving data bias improves generalization in binding affinity prediction
paper_authors: David Graber, Peter Stockinger, Fabian Meyer, Siddhartha Mishra, Claus Horn
